title: Firebase Authentication

sections.markdown:
**Think of Firebase Auth as a stadium's ticket-scanning gate.**

You show up at a big concert. Multiple ways to prove you belong:

- **Paper ticket** (email + password)
- **Ticket on your phone via QR code** (Google/Apple/social login)
- **SMS code sent to your phone** (phone OTP)
- **VIP wristband from another event** (custom token / your existing IdP)
- **General admission — walk-in guest badge** (anonymous)

Once you're inside, the scanner prints you a **wristband** valid for one hour (the JWT ID token). Every stall inside the stadium (Firestore, Cloud Storage, Realtime DB, Cloud Functions) trusts that wristband — no need to re-scan your ticket at each booth. When your hour is up, you go to a booth and get a fresh wristband (refresh token → new ID token) — no need to re-authenticate from scratch.

**Custom claims** are colored stickers on your wristband (VIP, staff, gold tier). Every stall reads them and decides what you can access. Written by the stadium office (Admin SDK on your server), NOT by you at the booth.

**Security Rules** are the rules each stall enforces: 'gold-tier wristbands can access this booth.' Written declaratively.

**Firebase Auth handles all the identity plumbing for you** — social provider OAuth flows, phone OTP delivery, session persistence, token refresh, secure cookie storage. You just react to auth state changes in your UI. **This is why every serious Flutter/Web app that needs auth reaches for Firebase Auth first.** It's free up to millions of users, integrates natively with all other Firebase services, and eliminates months of security-critical backend work.

**The one caveat:** DO NOT trust `currentUser` on the CLIENT for authorization decisions. The client is untrusted — anyone can patch your app. **Always enforce access in Security Rules or on the server** using the verified ID token. This is the #1 Firebase security mistake.

**Firebase Authentication** is Google's managed identity-as-a-service. Handles sign-up + sign-in for email/password, phone (OTP), Google, Apple, Facebook, Twitter/X, GitHub, anonymous, and custom tokens. On success, issues a **short-lived JWT ID token** (1-hour expiry) + a **long-lived refresh token**. Other Firebase services (Firestore, Storage, RTDB, Functions) verify the JWT automatically — no plumbing required. **Custom claims** (set via Admin SDK) enable role-based access enforced declaratively via **Security Rules**. Free tier covers most apps.

## Common mistakes
**Mistake 1: Trusting `auth.currentUser` on the CLIENT for authorization.** Anyone can patch the app. Always enforce in Security Rules or on the server via `verifyIdToken`.
**Mistake 2: Not verifying email.** Users can sign up with a stranger's email. Call `sendEmailVerification()`; gate features on `emailVerified`.
**Mistake 3: Setting claims from the client.** Custom claims are ADMIN-ONLY. Client can only set profile fields (displayName, photoURL).
**Mistake 4: Forgetting App Check.** Anyone can hit your Firebase project from an external client. App Check attests the request comes from your genuine app.
**Mistake 5: Skipping Apple Sign-In on iOS.** App Store REJECTS apps offering social login without Apple Sign-In.
**Mistake 6: Not force-refreshing after claims change.** Client uses stale token until next refresh; call `getIdToken(true)` after admin-side updates.
**Mistake 7: Storing sensitive tokens in shared_preferences.** Firebase persists them in Keychain / EncryptedSharedPreferences already — don't duplicate insecurely.
## Best practices
**1. Use `authStateChanges()` for reactive UI.** Never poll `currentUser`.
**2. Enforce access in Security Rules + server.** Never on the client.
**3. Verify email + phone.** Gate real features on `emailVerified`.
**4. Custom claims for roles/tenants.** RBAC without a users table.
**5. Enable App Check.** Blocks abuse from non-legitimate clients.
**6. Handle `FirebaseAuthException`.** Map error codes (`wrong-password`, `user-not-found`, etc.) to friendly messages.
**7. Anonymous → permanent upgrade.** `linkWithCredential` preserves the UID + all guest data.
**8. Rotate service account keys.** Never commit them to git; use Secret Manager or KMS.
## Practice programs
**Practice 1 (Easy) — Email/password.** Sign up, sign in, forgot-password flow.
**Practice 2 (Medium) — Google + Apple Sign-In.** Both flows; handle 'user cancelled'.
**Practice 3 (Medium) — Phone OTP.** Handle auto-retrieval on Android + manual entry.
**Practice 4 (Hard) — Anonymous → permanent.** `linkWithCredential`; verify UID preserved.
**Practice 5 (Hard) — Custom claims + rules.** Cloud Function sets role; Firestore Rules enforce access.
**Practice 6 (Expert) — Multi-tenant SaaS.** `tenantId` claim; per-tenant data isolation via rules; multi-factor auth.
## Interview Q&A

**Q1: How does Firebase Auth propagate identity to other Firebase services?**

**A:** On sign-in, Firebase Auth issues a **short-lived JWT ID token** (default 1-hour expiry, signed by Google's KMS). The Firebase Flutter SDK automatically attaches this token to every request to Firestore, Storage, RTDB, Cloud Functions. Each service **verifies the JWT signature** against Google's public keys + reads the `sub` (UID) and any custom claims. **Security Rules** then evaluate these against your rules (`request.auth.uid`, `request.auth.token.role`). No plumbing on your part. **Refresh:** the SDK also holds a long-lived **refresh token** (stored securely in Keychain/EncryptedSharedPreferences); when the ID token expires, the SDK trades the refresh token for a new ID token automatically. **The key insight:** identity flows end-to-end via ONE JWT — you never manually verify or forward tokens between services.

**Q2: What are custom claims and when do you use them?**

**A:** **Custom claims** are arbitrary key-value fields you attach to a user's JWT (roles, tenant IDs, subscription tier). Set via the **Admin SDK on your server** (`admin.auth().setCustomUserClaims(uid, {role: 'admin'})`) — never from the client. Embedded in the ID token → every Firebase service can read them via `request.auth.token.role` in Security Rules. **Use them for:** RBAC (admin/editor/viewer), multi-tenancy (`tenantId`), subscription gating (`plan: 'pro'`). **Advantages over a users table:** access decisions happen at the SERVICE (Firestore rule, Storage rule) with zero DB reads — declarative, fast, secure. **Caveats:** (1) 1000-byte limit per user — don't stuff full profile there. (2) Client must force-refresh (`getIdToken(true)`) or wait ~1 hour for changes to propagate. (3) Overuse leads to hidden coupling; keep claims minimal. **Interviewers love this — it's a textbook 'right way' to do authorization in a Firebase app.**

**Q3: How do you handle token refresh and revocation?**

**A:** **Refresh:** the Firebase SDK does it AUTOMATICALLY — every ~55 minutes it trades the refresh token for a fresh ID token in the background. No app code needed. **Force refresh:** `user.getIdToken(true)` — used after server-side custom claim changes to pick them up immediately. **Revocation** (harder — JWTs are stateless): (1) Server-side: call `admin.auth().revokeRefreshTokens(uid)` + set `checkRevoked: true` on `verifyIdToken` — any token issued before revocation time now fails. (2) Client-side: forcing sign-out on the compromised device is best-effort; a stolen ID token stays valid until its 1-hour expiry. **Best practice:** short-lived ID tokens + `revokeRefreshTokens` for compromised accounts + track suspicious sessions server-side. Also enable **App Check** to raise the bar for token abuse. Real-world security incidents like credential stuffing rely on these mechanisms — every senior interview covers this.

**Q4: How does anonymous auth work and when should you link accounts?**

**A:** **Anonymous auth** — `signInAnonymously()` — gives a user a UID + JWT without any credentials. Perfect for guest-mode features (cart, drafts) that later need to be preserved across devices. **Upgrade:** when the user signs up, call `currentUser.linkWithCredential(emailOrGoogleCred)` — the SAME UID now owns their guest data + is a permanent account. **Alternative** (bad UX): sign out the anonymous user, sign up fresh — user LOSES all guest data. **Use anonymous auth for:** e-commerce (cart before signup), read-only content apps (personalize before commit), games (start playing, sign up to save progress). **Caveat:** anonymous users still count toward your Firebase Auth billing tier + Firestore limits. Sweep abandoned anonymous accounts periodically. Also: security-rule-wise, treat anonymous users as low-trust (they can create infinite accounts).

**Q5: What's App Check and why enable it?**

**A:** **App Check** attests that requests to Firebase come from **your genuine app** (not a script, competitor, or attacker). Uses platform attestation: **DeviceCheck / App Attest** on iOS, **Play Integrity** on Android, **reCAPTCHA v3 / Enterprise** on web. The client fetches an attestation token; Firebase services reject requests without it (or with an invalid one). **Blocks:** scrapers, cost-attack floods (`Firebase Reads = $$$` at scale), credential-stuffing scripts, competitors reverse-engineering your API. **Setup:** 1 hour — install `firebase_app_check`, enable in console, gradually enforce per service. **Roll out in monitoring mode first** — verify legitimate traffic passes before enforcement. **Every production Firebase app should have this on.** Free tier: Play Integrity 10K/day; iOS unlimited; reCAPTCHA free tier generous.

**Q6: What are common Firebase Auth security mistakes?**

**A:** **(1) Trusting `currentUser` on the client for authorization** — the client is untrusted; enforce in Security Rules or server. **(2) Setting claims from the client** — impossible via SDK, but sometimes devs try to store 'role' in Firestore user document + trust it — that's just a mutable Firestore doc, not a claim. **(3) Skipping App Check** — abuse is a matter of time. **(4) No email verification** — spam signups, account takeover via typo'd email. **(5) Overly permissive rules** — `allow read, write: if request.auth != null;` = anyone signed in can read/write EVERYTHING. **(6) Service account key in git** — allows full Admin SDK access; rotate + move to Secret Manager. **(7) Not force-refreshing after custom claim changes** — user sees stale role until next auto-refresh. **(8) SMS OTP abuse** — enable reCAPTCHA + rate limits. **(9) Anonymous accounts never linked** — piles up + costs money. **(10) No MFA on admin roles** — high-privilege accounts should require multi-factor. Every senior interview drills these.

## Real-world usage

- **Every Flutter/Web/mobile app** with a small team + big auth needs.
- **Airbnb, Alibaba, Duolingo, NYT, Fabulous** — all use Firebase Auth.
- **Multi-tenant SaaS** — custom claims + rules is the go-to.
- **Games** — anonymous → link later.
- **NOT for** — enterprise SSO with custom IdP (use Auth0 or your own IdP + Firebase custom tokens as bridge).

## Advanced notes

- **Multi-factor auth (MFA)** — TOTP + SMS second factor; Firebase supports enrollment.
- **Identity Platform** — paid tier; adds SAML, OIDC federation, MFA, multi-tenancy.
- **`beforeCreate` + `beforeSignIn` blocking functions** — inject custom claims + reject sign-ins server-side.
- **Custom tokens** — sign a JWT with a service-account key; enable users to sign into Firebase from your own IdP (LDAP, custom OAuth).
- **User import** — bulk upload users from another system with `importUsers`; preserve password hashes.
- **Passwordless magic links** — `sendSignInLinkToEmail` + `signInWithEmailLink`.
- **Email link + password merge** — link a passwordless account to a password later.
- **Token TTL** — 1 hour default; adjustable via project settings (rarely).
- **`verifyIdToken({checkRevoked: true})`** — for high-security backends.
- **Emulator suite** — `firebase emulators:start` — test auth flows locally, no real Firebase.
- **User deletion** — `user.delete()`; also removes their data if you wire cleanup Functions.
- **Session cookies** for Web** — `createSessionCookie` on Admin SDK, longer-lived than 1h ID token.
- **Auth persistence** — SDK persists to Keychain / EncryptedSharedPreferences by default; can be changed.
- **Password policy** — enable min-length, complexity requirements via console.
